paragraphs: The paper develops a semi-bandit algorithm that adapts to two different kinds of environments. In stochastic environments, outcomes follow a statistical pattern; in adversarial environments, the learner must withstand strategically unfavorable outcomes. The algorithm does not need advance knowledge of which setting it faces or how many rounds it will run.

Its guarantees describe regret, the cumulative cost of learning compared with a reference choice. Regret grows logarithmically with the number of rounds in stochastic settings and at a square-root rate in adversarial settings. Achieving both with one algorithm avoids requiring the learner to select a regime in advance. The construction extends a multi-armed bandit approach using a new hybrid regularizer specifically designed for semi-bandit learning.

The results also address the leading constants in these bounds, establishing their optimality for two concrete semi-bandit problems as well as a worst-case criterion. Synthetic experiments support good performance across different environments. The paper additionally offers a preliminary extension to full bandit feedback; this extension is presented less definitively than the main semi-bandit results.
icml-2019-beating-stochastic-and-adversa.tldr: A single semi-bandit algorithm achieves strong stochastic and adversarial regret guarantees without knowing the environment type or time horizon.

paragraphs: CAVIA addresses meta-learning: learning across tasks so that a model can adapt quickly to a new one. It extends MAML by separating the parameters used for task adaptation from those that hold knowledge shared across tasks. This makes the location of task-specific change explicit within the model.

The method divides parameters into a shared component and a context component. Context parameters enter the model as additional inputs and are adjusted for individual tasks, while shared parameters are learned across tasks. At test time, adaptation changes only the context. The resulting low-dimensional representation describes the task through a compact set of adjustable values, making adaptation easier to interpret.

The authors report that CAVIA is less prone to meta-overfitting and easier to parallelize, with empirical improvements over MAML in regression, classification, and reinforcement learning. Their experiments also reveal a qualification about evaluation: some existing benchmarks require little adaptation. Consequently, the results speak both to the method's performance and to whether benchmark tasks meaningfully test the ability to adapt.
icml-2019-fast-context-adaptation-via-me.tldr: CAVIA adapts compact task-context parameters while sharing the rest of the model, empirically improving on MAML across several learning settings.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows offer flexible probability models for continuous variables and the possibility of generating outputs without a sequential autoregressive process. Applying those advantages to discrete sequences, such as text, is more difficult. This paper places the flow inside a latent-variable model, allowing continuous modeling machinery to support discrete observations.

The proposed model uses a variational autoencoder framework to learn two components together: a flow-based distribution in latent space and a probabilistic mapping from that space to discrete sequences. The authors find that the latent distribution needs to accommodate many distinct modes. They therefore introduce several flow architectures intended to increase flexibility and capture this multimodal structure.

Experiments examine character-level language modeling and polyphonic music generation. An autoregressive flow model can match a comparable autoregressive baseline, while a non-autoregressive version generates faster at a cost in modeling performance. The findings establish a practical tradeoff: latent flows can support discrete sequence generation, but the speed advantage reported for non-autoregressive generation comes with reduced performance.
icml-2019-latent-normalizing-flows-for-d.tldr: Latent normalizing flows model discrete sequences through a probabilistic decoder, with faster non-autoregressive generation trading off against performance.

paragraphs: The paper addresses visual recognition when new objects or environments provide too little labeled data to train a model from scratch. It brings together domain adaptation, few-shot learning, and zero-shot learning through a common image representation. The central aim is to make knowledge learned from the training environment usable in a new setting.

Each image is encoded as a compact probability vector whose entries describe prototypical part types. These prototypes are learned to represent the training data as a whole. A classifier then operates on this encoding. At test time, the encoder stays fixed, so adaptation occurs in the classifier rather than requiring the image representation itself to be relearned.

For few-shot learning, the classifier uses the limited available labels; for zero-shot learning, it uses new semantic attributes. This division gives the same representation a role across different forms of scarce supervision. Benchmark experiments report improvements over state-of-the-art methods specialized for domain adaptation, few-shot learning, and zero-shot learning, supporting the usefulness of the shared encoding across the evaluated settings.
icml-2019-learning-classifiers-for-targe.tldr: A fixed encoding of prototypical visual parts supports classifier adaptation with few labels or semantic attributes across several recognition settings.

paragraphs: Adaptive data analysis lets earlier results influence later questions asked of the same data. Generalization guarantees can become pessimistic when analysts are allowed to exploit every previous answer adversarially. This paper develops models of more restricted analysts, aiming to explain why ordinary adaptive analysis may behave better than that worst-case picture suggests.

The analyst is represented as an unknown dynamical system: revealed information changes its internal knowledge, which determines subsequent statistical queries. Control-theoretic restrictions describe how information persists. One models recency bias, limiting the use of distant information. Another models anchoring bias, giving greater weight to initial information. Quantitative parameters control the strength of these restrictions.

The resulting guarantees vary smoothly between non-adaptive bounds and the best-known fully adaptive bounds. This creates a spectrum of analysts with different capacities to reuse information. The authors also show that their definitions encompass gradient descent in various settings, offering an interpretation of why this adaptive optimization method can overfit less than unrestricted adaptive-analysis theory might lead one to expect.
icml-2019-natural-analysts-in-adaptive-d.tldr: Dynamical models of analysts with recency or anchoring biases yield generalization guarantees between non-adaptive and fully adaptive extremes.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent depends on a stepsize that controls how far each update moves. Choosing it manually can require substantial tuning, even though the purpose is simply to make optimization converge quickly. This paper treats stepsize selection as a learning problem that runs alongside optimization of the original objective.

The authors introduce surrogate losses that turn stepsize learning for a smooth, non-convex objective into an online convex optimization problem. This separation matters: the original objective remains non-convex, but the auxiliary decisions about update size can use tools developed for convex online learning. No-regret algorithms then compute stepsizes as the optimization proceeds, using the surrogate formulation to guide those choices.

The resulting SGD method tunes its own stepsizes and has convergence-rate guarantees that adapt automatically to the level of stochastic noise. Thus, the contribution connects an online learning mechanism for update sizes to a theoretical property of the optimization process. The stated setting is smooth non-convex stochastic optimization, and the guarantee concerns convergence rates that respond to noise.
icml-2019-surrogate-losses-for-online-le.tldr: Surrogate losses let online convex learning tune SGD stepsizes during optimization, yielding convergence guarantees that adapt to stochastic noise.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how the directional structure of noise affects stochastic gradient descent. Its framework studies gradient-based optimization with unbiased noise and includes both SGD and standard Langevin dynamics. The question is how noise helps an optimizer leave minima and how that behavior contributes to implicit regularization.

The authors derive an indicator that relates escape efficiency to the alignment between noise covariance and the curvature of the loss. Covariance describes how noise varies across directions, while curvature describes the local shape of the objective. From this indicator, they establish two conditions under which structured noise is better for escaping than isotropic noise, which treats directions uniformly.

They further show that SGD's anisotropic noise satisfies these conditions, helping it move away from sharp, poor minima toward flatter, more stable ones. Such minima are described as typically generalizing well, rather than guaranteeing good generalization in every case. Experiments compare this directional noise with full gradient descent plus isotropic diffusion and support the benefits identified by the analysis.
icml-2019-the-anisotropic-noise-in-stoch.tldr: The alignment of SGD noise with loss curvature helps explain its ability to escape sharp minima and favor flatter solutions.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning problems often involve several competing objectives whose numerical values use different units or scales. This makes preferences difficult to express directly: the numerical size of an objective can interfere with the intended tradeoff. The paper proposes a way to specify preferences that is invariant to these scale differences.

The method learns a separate action distribution for each objective. It then combines those distributions and uses supervised learning to fit a parametric policy to the combination. This moves the combination step into the space of action distributions, providing a common basis for bringing together objectives whose original numerical measurements may be difficult to compare.

The authors demonstrate the approach on high-dimensional robotics tasks in both real and simulated settings. Varying the preferences traces out nondominated solutions: choices where improving one objective cannot be achieved without sacrificing another. The results show how the framework can expose different effective tradeoffs, allowing preference changes to select among policies rather than forcing every objective into one native numerical scale.
icml-2020-a-distributional-view-on-multi.tldr: Combining objective-specific action distributions enables scale-invariant preferences and effective tradeoffs in multi-objective reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Archetypal analysis describes data using mixtures of extreme representative points, called archetypes. These points lie on the data's convex hull, and the mixture weights form convex combinations. The paper develops a greedy algorithm that uses this geometric structure to make finding archetypes more computationally efficient and scalable.

The proposed method, GAA, learns archetypes through sparse projections of the data. In the transformed space, it repeatedly selects subsets using the sparsity of convex representations. Sparsity focuses attention on representations supported by relatively few components. This connects the search for archetypes to the geometry of how data points can be expressed as mixtures.

The authors report a substantially faster convergence rate and extend the algorithm to robust and kernel versions of archetypal analysis. Experiments on classification and data visualization or categorization show considerably faster computation with performance comparable to existing approaches. The practical finding is that exploiting the representation's geometry can reduce computational expense while retaining useful downstream behavior in the tasks evaluated.
icml-2020-a-geometric-approach-to-archet.tldr: A greedy geometric algorithm uses sparse projections to accelerate archetypal analysis while retaining comparable performance on evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: The paper studies reinforcement learning from a fixed collection of previously logged interactions. Its dataset contains the full replay experience of a DQN agent across 60 Atari games. The authors show that recent off-policy deep reinforcement learning algorithms can exceed the fully trained DQN agent's performance while learning exclusively from those stored experiences.

They also introduce Random Ensemble Mixture, or REM, to improve generalization in this offline setting. REM maintains multiple Q-value estimates and enforces optimal Bellman consistency on random convex combinations of them. These combinations are weighted mixtures whose weights sum to one. The training constraint therefore applies across random mixtures of value estimates.

Offline REM outperforms strong reinforcement learning baselines on the DQN replay dataset. Ablation studies connect these positive outcomes to dataset size, dataset diversity, and algorithm choice. The broader conclusion is conditional: robust algorithms can produce high-quality policies from sufficiently large and diverse offline data. The released replay dataset also provides a benchmark for studying that possibility.
icml-2020-an-optimistic-perspective-on-o.tldr: REM and other off-policy algorithms learn strong Atari policies from fixed replay data, with success tied to data size, diversity, and algorithm choice.

paragraphs: The paper asks how multiple controllers for a dynamical system can be combined to improve control performance. A controller determines actions for a system that evolves over time, so aggregation must be considered in an online control setting. The objective is to turn a collection of weak controllers into a more accurate combined controller.

The authors propose a boosting framework for this purpose. Its central contribution is an efficient algorithm that combines weak controllers and provides a proof of improved accuracy. This makes controller aggregation an algorithmic problem with a theoretical performance result. The role of boosting is to organize the combination so that the resulting controller improves on the weak control components.

Empirical evaluations across several control settings support the theoretical findings. Together, the analysis and experiments establish the paper's stated contribution: boosting can provide a principled framework for improving control through aggregation. The result concerns the combined controller's accuracy, with computational efficiency also included in the main algorithmic claim.
icml-2020-boosting-for-control-of-dynami.tldr: An efficient boosting algorithm combines weak controllers into a provably more accurate controller, with empirical support across control settings.

paragraphs: Local differential privacy can substantially reduce the usefulness of data. The paper identifies one source of that cost: its standard definition treats every possible data value as equally sensitive. The proposed context-aware framework allows privacy requirements to vary across the domain, so protection can reflect differences in sensitivity.

For binary domains, the authors provide a universally optimal privatization scheme and relate it to established randomized-response methods. For domains with more possible values, they study block-structured and high-low privacy requirements, motivated by location and web-search applications. They analyze how accurately an underlying discrete distribution can be estimated under these forms of protection.

The results include schemes with optimal sample requirements, efficient communication, and information-theoretic lower bounds. Worst-case analysis and experiments on location check-ins show substantially better accuracy at the same sample count. The improvement comes from changing how privacy constraints are allocated across values; it therefore depends on the framework's explicit recognition that different parts of the data domain can require different protection.
icml-2020-context-aware-local-differenti.tldr: Allowing privacy requirements to vary with data sensitivity yields sample-optimal estimation schemes and improved accuracy under context-aware local privacy.

paragraphs: Useful predictive uncertainty should accomplish two things: include the true target with high probability and distinguish predictions deserving high confidence from those deserving less. The paper argues that strong predictive accuracy alone does not supply these properties. It also identifies potential shortcomings of Bayesian credible intervals and approximate posterior inference for these particular goals.

The proposed discriminative jackknife is a frequentist procedure based on leave-one-out reasoning. It uses influence functions of the model's loss functional to construct predictive confidence intervals. This ties uncertainty estimation to how the fitted model responds to changes in its training data, giving the procedure a basis in the variability captured by jackknife estimation.

The authors state that the method provides both coverage and discrimination between confidence levels. It applies to a broad range of deep learning models and can be added after training without changing that training or reducing predictive accuracy. Regression experiments show competitive performance against Bayesian and non-Bayesian alternatives, supporting the practical usefulness of the proposed interval estimates.
icml-2020-discriminative-jackknife-quant.tldr: The discriminative jackknife uses influence functions to add predictive confidence intervals with coverage and instance-level discrimination to trained deep models.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover causal structure when some variables are unobserved while keeping intervention costs low. It distinguishes two cost models. In the linear model, intervention cost depends linearly on the selected variables. In the identity model, every intervention costs the same, making the number of interventions the relevant quantity.

Under linear costs, the algorithm identifies ancestral relations in the underlying causal graph. These describe whether one variable is upstream of another through causal paths. Its intervention cost is at most twice the optimum. Under additional restrictions, the approximation factor improves to one plus any positive epsilon, bringing the cost arbitrarily close to optimal within that setting.

Under identity costs, the result concerns recovery of the entire graph, including latent variables. The authors introduce p-colliders, a particular collider structure arising through specified conditioning, and bound intervention counts using the maximum number between any pair of nodes. The two results therefore connect intervention expense to different recovery goals and different structural features of the causal problem.
icml-2020-efficient-intervention-design-.tldr: Intervention-design guarantees relate causal recovery with latent variables to either near-optimal variable-dependent costs or graph-dependent intervention counts.

paragraphs: The paper addresses exploration and exploitation in linear-quadratic control, where a learner must control a system while learning its dynamics. Optimistic methods choose favorable plausible dynamics within a confidence region. The challenge addressed here is computing such a controller efficiently while preserving strong guarantees about the cumulative cost of learning.

The authors relax the optimistic optimization into a constrained extended control problem. An additional control variable implicitly selects dynamics within the confidence interval. They then use a Lagrangian formulation and prove strong duality, establishing the connection needed to solve the relaxed problem through its dual. This reformulation turns the optimistic computation into a tractable sequence of control calculations.

An epsilon-optimistic controller requires solving at most a logarithmic number of Riccati equations in inverse epsilon. The authors also prove that the relaxation preserves learning performance, recovering square-root regret up to logarithmic factors. The contribution joins computational efficiency with a worst-case optimal regret guarantee, addressing both the expense of selecting controls and the cost incurred while learning.
icml-2020-efficient-optimistic-explorati.tldr: A Lagrangian relaxation makes optimistic linear-quadratic control computationally efficient while preserving square-root regret up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks make predictions from sequences, but decisions based on those predictions also need an indication of uncertainty. The paper develops a frequentist approach that can be applied to any RNN architecture without changing its training or compromising predictive accuracy. Its uncertainty intervals come with theoretical coverage guarantees.

The method draws on jackknife resampling, estimating variability by considering what would happen if portions of the training data were removed. Because sequence observations are temporally correlated, the removed units are blocks of data. Predictions from models trained on the remaining data define the sampling variability used to construct uncertainty estimates.

Exhaustively retraining an RNN for these removals would be expensive. The authors instead use influence functions to estimate how deleting each block changes the learned parameters. This approximates the effects needed for blockwise jackknife estimation without carrying out every retraining operation. An application using critical-care data demonstrates the usefulness of the uncertainty estimates for sequential decision-making.
icml-2020-frequentist-uncertainty-in-rec.tldr: Blockwise influence functions estimate jackknife uncertainty for RNN predictions without exhaustive retraining, with theoretical coverage guarantees.

paragraphs: Predictors can fail when correlations learned during training change in a new environment. Invariant risk minimization uses multiple training environments to seek predictors that remain valid across them, reducing reliance on spurious features. This paper reformulates that search as an ensemble game played among the environments.

The key theoretical result equates the game's Nash equilibria with invariant predictors for any finite number of environments. The equivalence includes nonlinear classifiers and transformations. A Nash equilibrium describes a configuration where no player benefits from changing its own strategy alone; here, that equilibrium condition provides a game-theoretic characterization of the desired predictors.

The reformulation leads to a simple training algorithm based on best-response dynamics. In the reported experiments, it achieves similar or better accuracy with substantially lower variance than the earlier bilevel optimization approach. The method also retains the earlier framework's generalization guarantees over a large set of environments. The paper thus connects a theoretical equivalence to a training procedure with favorable empirical behavior.
icml-2020-invariant-risk-minimization-ga.tldr: Casting invariant prediction as a game yields an equilibrium characterization and a simple training algorithm with lower empirical variance.

paragraphs: Observational data can leave several directed causal graphs consistent with the same conditional independencies. Such graphs form a Markov equivalence class. Counting the graphs in that class measures the remaining ambiguity and helps characterize the difficulty of identifying the true causal graph through interventions. This paper makes that counting and experiment-design process more efficient.

LazyIter efficiently iterates over possible equivalence classes given intervention results. The authors use this procedure both to compute class sizes and to design experiments in active and passive learning settings. For sparse graphs, the counting algorithm improves time complexity over previous work by a factor proportional to the number of variables.

Combining the approach with dynamic programming also produces an optimal algorithm for passive experiment design. Experiments show improvements over state-of-the-art methods for both class-size computation and experiment design. The contribution matters because handling the remaining graph ambiguity efficiently supports two related operations: measuring how much uncertainty remains and choosing experiments intended to resolve causal structure.
icml-2020-lazyiter-a-fast-algorithm-for-.tldr: LazyIter accelerates counting observationally equivalent causal graphs and supports improved intervention design, including optimal passive design.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning can learn procedures for combinatorial optimization, but sequential construction can become a bottleneck. Existing solvers considered in this paper use a number of stages proportional to the number of elements in the solution. On large graphs, that relationship limits how quickly a learned solver can finish constructing its answer.

Learning what to defer changes the organization of those decisions. The agent learns how to distribute element-level choices across stages, adaptively increasing or decreasing the number of stages it uses. Deferral becomes part of the learned strategy: the solver controls which decisions occur now and which are left for later as it constructs a solution.

The authors apply this framework to maximum independent set, which seeks a largest collection of vertices with no edges between selected vertices. They report substantial improvements over the current state-of-the-art deep reinforcement learning approach. On graphs with millions of vertices, the method can also outperform conventional solvers under a limited time budget, making decision scheduling relevant to practical large-scale performance.
icml-2020-learning-what-to-defer-for-max.tldr: Learning which graph decisions to defer lets a reinforcement learning solver adapt its stage count and improve large-scale maximum independent set performance.

paragraphs: Different mathematical measures capture differences between probability distributions in different ways. This paper studies the relationship between f-divergences, including Kullback-Leibler divergence, and integral probability metrics, including total variation and maximum mean discrepancy. Understanding these connections makes it possible to relate measures commonly used in estimation and optimization.

The authors approach the problem through convex duality. Starting with a tight variational representation of an f-divergence, they derive a generalized moment-generating function. This object exactly characterizes the strongest lower bound on that divergence obtainable as a function of a specified integral probability metric. The result identifies the best such bound rather than merely supplying one valid inequality.

The characterization yields new bounds for metrics defined through classes of unbounded functions. It also recovers established results for bounded and subgaussian functions, including Pinsker's inequality and Hoeffding's lemma, within one framework. The contribution is therefore both a source of new inequalities and a common mathematical explanation for several existing relationships between distributional measures.
icml-2020-optimal-bounds-between-f-diver.tldr: Convex duality yields an exact characterization of optimal lower bounds linking f-divergences to integral probability metrics.

paragraphs: The paper studies ranking from pairwise comparisons when some observations have been maliciously altered. Truthful comparisons initially follow the Bradley-Terry-Luce model, which associates items with underlying scores. The goal is to recover those scores even after an adversary contaminates part of the comparison data.

The contamination model gives the adversary extensive power: it knows both the truthful observations and the true model parameters, and can insert, delete, or modify data points. The authors characterize how much corruption can be present while still leaving the true parameters uniquely identifiable. This addresses whether the data can distinguish the correct scores before considering how an algorithm should estimate them.

They then introduce a pruning algorithm with a guarantee of cleaning adversarial corruption under conditions on data generation and corruption. Experiments on synthetic and real data support the analysis: previous algorithms are vulnerable to small contamination levels, while the proposed method can remove a reasonably large amount. These findings support robustness within the stated model and conditions.
icml-2020-rank-aggregation-from-pairwise.tldr: The paper characterizes identifiability under adversarially corrupted pairwise comparisons and gives a conditionally guaranteed pruning method for robust ranking.

paragraphs: An imperfect environment model can still help a reinforcement learning agent, but planning with it can also damage learning. The paper investigates selective planning: using the model in regions where its predictions help and avoiding regions where they mislead. Making this distinction requires an informative estimate of predictive uncertainty.

The authors emphasize that uncertainty has multiple sources. Uncertain parameters are one source, but the model may also lack the capacity to represent the environment adequately. Prior selective-planning work has focused on parameter uncertainty. This study highlights model inadequacy as a separate concern that a useful uncertainty estimate should also be able to signal.

The paper shows that heteroscedastic regression, which allows predictive variability to differ across inputs, can signal uncertainty associated with model inadequacy. That signal complements uncertainty detected by methods focused on parameters. The conclusion is a qualified research direction: accounting for both sources may support more effective selective planning than considering either alone, because an imperfect model's usefulness can vary across the state space.
icml-2020-selective-dyna-style-planning-.tldr: Heteroscedastic regression can flag model inadequacy, complementing parameter uncertainty when deciding where an imperfect environment model is useful for planning.

paragraphs: Some optimization problems require differentiating a function whose value is itself obtained by minimizing another function. When that inner minimum has no closed form, an iterative algorithm approximates it. The paper compares two ways to estimate the outer gradient: using an analytic formula that treats the approximation as exact, or differentiating through the iterative algorithm.

The analysis relates gradient-estimation error to the remaining optimization error. Asymptotically, the automatic-differentiation estimator has error close to the square of the analytic estimator's error. This is the reported super-efficiency phenomenon: improving the approximate inner solution can yield a substantially more accurate gradient when differentiation follows the computation that produced it.

That advantage depends strongly on convergence of the algorithm's Jacobian, which describes the sensitivity of its outputs. The authors analyze gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent and derive estimator convergence rates. Numerical experiments on toy problems and Wasserstein barycenters support the analysis. They also examine computational complexity and give guidance for choosing between the two estimators.
icml-2020-super-efficiency-of-automatic-.tldr: Differentiating through an approximate minimization algorithm can yield asymptotically much smaller gradient error, with behavior tied to Jacobian convergence.

paragraphs: Double descent describes test error that falls, rises near the capacity needed to fit training data, and then falls again as capacity increases further. This paper asks whether that picture captures the behavior of neural networks deeply into the overparameterized regime. It argues that simpler theoretical models can miss relevant structure.

The authors provide a precise high-dimensional asymptotic analysis of kernel regression using the neural tangent kernel. This kernel characterizes the behavior of wide neural networks optimized with gradient descent. The analysis examines generalization in this structured setting, allowing the relationship between parameter count, dataset size, and test error to have more than one characteristic scale.

The results show that test error can remain nonmonotonic well beyond the interpolation threshold. Additional peaks and descents can appear when parameter count scales quadratically with dataset size. Thus, an initial improvement in the overparameterized regime need not imply uninterrupted improvement with further growth. The findings refine the double-descent picture within the paper's neural-tangent-kernel asymptotic analysis.
icml-2020-the-neural-tangent-kernel-in-h.tldr: A high-dimensional neural tangent kernel analysis reveals that test error can exhibit additional peaks and descents deep in the overparameterized regime.

paragraphs: Infinite-width limits make neural networks easier to analyze by relating their outputs to Gaussian processes. The paper identifies a missing capability in infinite Bayesian networks with fixed kernels: they cannot learn representations from data. Their kernels depend only on network hyperparameters, restricting the flexibility available during learning.

The authors suggest this loss of representation learning as a possible explanation for inferior infinite-network performance reported in prior work. They derive analytic results for the distribution of representations and for representation learning in finite deep linear networks. These results describe aspects of finite networks that the corresponding fixed-kernel infinite limit does not retain.

Empirical comparisons show that representations in architectures such as ResNets trained with SGD are closer to those suggested by the finite deep linear analysis than by the corresponding infinite network. Motivated by this evidence, the authors introduce infinite networks with bottlenecks. These models are intended to retain the analytical tractability of infinite networks while allowing representations to be learned.
icml-2020-why-bigger-is-not-always-bette.tldr: Finite-network representation learning helps explain a limitation of fixed-kernel infinite networks and motivates infinite networks with learnable bottleneck representations.
